claim: Tenofovir 1% gel suppressed 505 genes and induced 137 genes in 9 cm rectal biopsies after 7 days of treatment relative to enrollment biopsies.
source: Relative to enrollment biopsies, after 7 days of treatment, tenofovir 1% gel suppressed 505 genes and induced 137 genes in the 9 cm biopsies, whereas the detergent N-9, a transient mucosal toxin, suppressed 56 genes and induced 60 genes (log2 fold expression change ≥ 0.5 for induction or ≤ −0.5 for suppression, FDR ≤ 0.05) (Figure 1A,B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by microarray data analysis with specific statistical thresholds (FDR ≤ 0.05, log2 fold change criteria) and shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Nonoxynol-9 (N-9) 2% gel suppressed 56 genes and induced 60 genes in 9 cm rectal biopsies after 7 days of treatment.
source: Relative to enrollment biopsies, after 7 days of treatment, tenofovir 1% gel suppressed 505 genes and induced 137 genes in the 9 cm biopsies, whereas the detergent N-9, a transient mucosal toxin, suppressed 56 genes and induced 60 genes (log2 fold expression change ≥ 0.5 for induction or ≤ −0.5 for suppression, FDR ≤ 0.05) (Figure 1A,B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by microarray data analysis with specific statistical thresholds and shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: 15 suppressed and 4 induced genes were common to both tenofovir and N-9 treatment.
source: 15 suppressed and 4 induced genes were common to tenofovir and N-9 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HEC gel and no treatment arms resulted in 16 and 23 gene changes, respectively.
source: In the HEC gel and no treatment arms, 16 and 23 genes changed (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tenofovir 1% gel affected more genes after 7 days of treatment than after a single application.
source: Tenofovir 1% gel affected more genes after 7 days of treatment than after a single application and more genes in 9 cm than in 15 cm biopsies (Figure 1B), with significant correlations between expression changes at 9 cm and 15 cm (suppression: Spearman rho = 0.4775 [95% CI: 0.4051–0.5440]; p < 0.001, Figure 1C; induction: Spearman rho = 0.427 [95% CI: 0.2840–0.5514]; p < 0.001, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene expression changes at different time points shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tenofovir 1% gel affected more genes in 9 cm than in 15 cm rectal biopsies.
source: Tenofovir 1% gel affected more genes after 7 days of treatment than after a single application and more genes in 9 cm than in 15 cm biopsies (Figure 1B), with significant correlations between expression changes at 9 cm and 15 cm (suppression: Spearman rho = 0.4775 [95% CI: 0.4051–0.5440]; p < 0.001, Figure 1C; induction: Spearman rho = 0.427 [95% CI: 0.2840–0.5514]; p < 0.001, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene expression changes at different biopsy sites shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is a significant correlation between gene suppression at 9 cm and 15 cm rectal biopsies (Spearman rho = 0.4775, p < 0.001).
source: Tenofovir 1% gel affected more genes after 7 days of treatment than after a single application and more genes in 9 cm than in 15 cm biopsies (Figure 1B), with significant correlations between expression changes at 9 cm and 15 cm (suppression: Spearman rho = 0.4775 [95% CI: 0.4051–0.5440]; p < 0.001, Figure 1C; induction: Spearman rho = 0.427 [95% CI: 0.2840–0.5514]; p < 0.001, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a significant correlation between gene induction at 9 cm and 15 cm rectal biopsies (Spearman rho = 0.427, p < 0.001).
source: Tenofovir 1% gel affected more genes after 7 days of treatment than after a single application and more genes in 9 cm than in 15 cm biopsies (Figure 1B), with significant correlations between expression changes at 9 cm and 15 cm (suppression: Spearman rho = 0.4775 [95% CI: 0.4051–0.5440]; p < 0.001, Figure 1C; induction: Spearman rho = 0.427 [95% CI: 0.2840–0.5514]; p < 0.001, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed genes more strongly than N-9 by fold change (median 0.505 vs 0.627-fold; p < 0.001).
source: By fold change of the individual genes, tenofovir suppressed genes more strongly than N-9 (median 0.505 vs 0.627-fold; p < 0.001), but induced genes less strongly (1.58 vs 1.69-fold; p < 0.001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of fold changes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tenofovir induced genes less strongly than N-9 by fold change (1.58 vs 1.69-fold; p < 0.001).
source: By fold change of the individual genes, tenofovir suppressed genes more strongly than N-9 (median 0.505 vs 0.627-fold; p < 0.001), but induced genes less strongly (1.58 vs 1.69-fold; p < 0.001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of fold changes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All 15 genes selected for RT-ddPCR confirmation (9 induced and 6 suppressed) showed expression changes consistent with microarray predictions.
source: The mRNA copy numbers of all 15 genes increased or decreased as predicted from the microarray data between baseline and time point VII (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 2A,B confirming microarray results.

claim: Expression changes for all 15 genes assessed by microarray and RT-ddPCR were statistically significant (p < 0.01 for all genes except TRIM5 [p = 0.02]).
source: Expression changes for all 15 genes assessed by microarray and RT-ddPCR were statistically significant (p < 0.01 for all genes except TRIM5 [p = 0.02]).
evidence: Supported by combined statistical analysis of microarray and RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CD7+ infiltrating T lymphocytes increased fivefold in the rectal mucosa after 7 days of tenofovir 1% gel use (mean fold change 5.0, 95% CI 2.46–10.1, p < 0.001).
source: Consistent with the gene expression studies, infiltrating T lymphocytes increased twofold to fivefold in the mucosa (mean fold change 5.0, 95% CI 2.46–10.1, p < 0.001 for CD7+; 2.44, 1.17–5.11, p = 0.023 for CD3+), whereas IL-10+ columnar epithelial cells decreased by more than half (0.36, 0.18–0.79, p = 0.017), between baseline and following 7 days of tenofovir 1% gel use.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CD3+ infiltrating T lymphocytes increased 2.44-fold in the rectal mucosa after 7 days of tenofovir 1% gel use (95% CI 1.17–5.11, p = 0.023).
source: Consistent with the gene expression studies, infiltrating T lymphocytes increased twofold to fivefold in the mucosa (mean fold change 5.0, 95% CI 2.46–10.1, p < 0.001 for CD7+; 2.44, 1.17–5.11, p = 0.023 for CD3+), whereas IL-10+ columnar epithelial cells decreased by more than half (0.36, 0.18–0.79, p = 0.017), between baseline and following 7 days of tenofovir 1% gel use.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: IL-10+ columnar epithelial cells decreased by more than half after 7 days of tenofovir 1% gel use (0.36, 0.18–0.79, p = 0.017).
source: Consistent with the gene expression studies, infiltrating T lymphocytes increased twofold to fivefold in the mucosa (mean fold change 5.0, 95% CI 2.46–10.1, p < 0.001 for CD7+; 2.44, 1.17–5.11, p = 0.023 for CD3+), whereas IL-10+ columnar epithelial cells decreased by more than half (0.36, 0.18–0.79, p = 0.017), between baseline and following 7 days of tenofovir 1% gel use.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Tenofovir treatment increased the intensity of ubiquitin D expression in rectal epithelial cells (p = 0.007).
source: Ubiquitin D was widely expressed in all biopsies, but tenofovir treatment increased the intensity of its expression (p = 0.007), as predicted by the microarrays.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Tenofovir 1% gel had a ratio of induced to suppressed genes of 0.116 for nuclear products (17 genes up-regulated to 146 down).
source: Tenofovir 1% gel was more suppressive than stimulatory, with a ratio of induced to suppressed genes in the 9-cm rectal biopsies of 0.116 (17 genes up-regulated to 146 down) for nuclear products.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Genes encoding secreted proteins were more often induced than suppressed by tenofovir, with a ratio of 2.33 (35 genes up-regulated to 15 down; χ2 p < 0.001).
source: However, genes encoding secreted proteins were more often induced than suppressed (Figure 3A), with a ratio of 2.33 (35 genes up-regulated to 15 down; χ2 p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A with statistical significance by Chi-square test.

claim: Tenofovir induced chemokines CCL2, CCL19, CCL21, CCL23, CXCL9, and CXCL13.
source: Noteworthy among induced genes for secreted products were the chemokines CCL2, CCL19, CCL21, CCL23, CXCL9, and CXCL13 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Tenofovir increased transcripts of leukocyte-specific cell surface markers CD2, CD3D, CD7, CD8A, CD19, CD52, CD53, CCR6, and CCR7.
source: Correspondingly, transcripts of a number of leukocyte-specific cell surface markers increased, specifically CD2, CD3D, CD7, CD8A, CD19, CD52, CD53, CCR6, and CCR7.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed transcription factors and co-factors including CREB1, CREBBP, NFAT5, and many zinc finger proteins.
source: Among suppressed genes with products localizing to the cell nucleus, we identified a large number of known or putative transcription factors and their co-factors, including CREB1 (CAMP responsive element-binding protein 1) and CREBBP (CREB-binding protein), both activators of IL-10 transcription (Woodgett and Ohashi, 2005; Alvarez et al., 2009), NFAT5 (nuclear factor of activated T cells 5) (Neuhofer, 2010), and many zinc finger proteins (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A and cited literature on gene functions.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed genes important for regulation of transcription and translation, as well as biological processes involving TGF-β, epithelial structure organization, regulation of cell proliferation, and apoptosis.
source: Tenofovir 1% gel also suppressed genes important for regulation of transcription and translation, as well as biological processes involving transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), epithelial structure organization, regulation of cell proliferation, and apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed genes important for mitochondrial function, including PNPT1 and OPA3.
source: Lastly, tenofovir 1% gel suppressed genes important for mitochondrial function, including PNPT1 (polyribonucleotide nucleotidyltransferase 1) (Wang et al., 2010) and OPA3 (optic atrophy 3) (Misaka et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data with citations to literature on gene functions.

claim: KIAA0101 and ubiquitin D were strongly induced genes with nuclear products.
source: Among the few genes with nuclear products that were strongly induced, KIAA0101 and ubiquitin D were notable (Yu et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2003; Hosokawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data with citations to literature on these genes.

claim: Pre-processed microarray expression data from three vaginal cell cultures were extremely consistent (mean Pearson correlation coefficient 0.9912).
source: Pre-processed microarray expression data were extremely consistent between the three vaginal cell cultures (mean Pearson correlation coefficient 0.9912; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of microarray data.

claim: Tenofovir's effects on purified vaginal epithelial cells were similar to its effects on the rectal mucosa.
source: Tenofovir's effects on the purified vaginal epithelial cells (Figure 3B) were similar to its effects on the rectal mucosa (Figure 3A), but, as expected, changes likely driven by leukocytes in the biopsies were not seen in the purified epithelial cells, or were differently regulated.
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene expression patterns shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: In vaginal epithelial cells, tenofovir did not significantly change chemokine, chemokine receptor, and CD genes.
source: In the epithelial cells, tenofovir did not significantly change chemokine, chemokine receptor, and cluster of differentiation (CD) genes, and it suppressed ISG 15 (interferon-stimulated gene 15) and MX1 (myxovirus resistance 1), which were induced in the biopsies.
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene expression between vaginal epithelial cells and rectal biopsies.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed ISG15 and MX1 in vaginal epithelial cells, which were induced in rectal biopsies.
source: In the epithelial cells, tenofovir did not significantly change chemokine, chemokine receptor, and cluster of differentiation (CD) genes, and it suppressed ISG 15 (interferon-stimulated gene 15) and MX1 (myxovirus resistance 1), which were induced in the biopsies.
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene expression between vaginal epithelial cells and rectal biopsies.

claim: The number of genes affected by tenofovir in vaginal epithelial cells was initially higher with 500 μM than with 50 μM, but equalized after 14 days of culture.
source: The number of genes affected was initially higher with 500 μM than with 50 μM tenofovir, but equalized after 14 days of culture (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by time-course gene expression data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DSP mRNA copies significantly decreased in vaginal epithelial cells during 7 days of tenofovir treatment.
source: Next, we confirmed the expression changes of select genes by ddPCR with vaginal epithelial cells from four healthy women: mRNA copies of DSP (desmoplakin) and IL-10 significantly decreased, and KIAA0101 significantly increased during 7 days of tenofovir treatment, as seen in the microarray data (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IL-10 mRNA copies significantly decreased in vaginal epithelial cells during 7 days of tenofovir treatment.
source: Next, we confirmed the expression changes of select genes by ddPCR with vaginal epithelial cells from four healthy women: mRNA copies of DSP (desmoplakin) and IL-10 significantly decreased, and KIAA0101 significantly increased during 7 days of tenofovir treatment, as seen in the microarray data (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: KIAA0101 mRNA copies significantly increased in vaginal epithelial cells during 7 days of tenofovir treatment.
source: Next, we confirmed the expression changes of select genes by ddPCR with vaginal epithelial cells from four healthy women: mRNA copies of DSP (desmoplakin) and IL-10 significantly decreased, and KIAA0101 significantly increased during 7 days of tenofovir treatment, as seen in the microarray data (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IL-10 transcripts were virtually eliminated at 7 days of tenofovir treatment in vaginal epithelial cells (p = 0.002 and p = 0.003 for 50 and 500 μM, respectively).
source: In fact, IL-10 transcripts were virtually eliminated at 7 days (p = 0.002 and p = 0.003 for 50 and 500 μM, respectively), and KIAA0101 increased more than 10-fold at 500 μM tenofovir (p = 0.005).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: KIAA0101 increased more than 10-fold at 500 μM tenofovir in vaginal epithelial cells (p = 0.005).
source: In fact, IL-10 transcripts were virtually eliminated at 7 days (p = 0.002 and p = 0.003 for 50 and 500 μM, respectively), and KIAA0101 increased more than 10-fold at 500 μM tenofovir (p = 0.005).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IL-10 protein significantly decreased in vaginal epithelial cells after tenofovir treatment (p = 0.007 and p < 0.001 for 50 and 500 μM, respectively).
source: By ELISA of cell lysates, IL-10 protein also decreased significantly (n = 4 cell lines; p = 0.007 and p < 0.001 for 50 and 500 μM, respectively) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tenofovir treatment of primary vaginal epithelial cells in vitro mostly impacted the same biological processes as it did in the rectum in vivo.
source: Tenofovir treatment of primary vaginal epithelial cells in vitro mostly impacted the same biological processes as it did in the rectum in vivo (Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figures 4D and 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed genes important for keratinocyte differentiation and cellular innate immunity in vaginal epithelial cells.
source: Additionally, it suppressed genes important for keratinocyte differentiation and cellular innate immunity, and induced genes involved in DNA damage repair.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tenofovir induced genes involved in DNA damage repair in vaginal epithelial cells.
source: Additionally, it suppressed genes important for keratinocyte differentiation and cellular innate immunity, and induced genes involved in DNA damage repair.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tenofovir enhanced vaginal epithelial cell proliferation and/or cell survival in vitro (p = 0.02).
source: Furthermore, tenofovir enhanced vaginal epithelial cell proliferation and/or cell survival in vitro (p = 0.02) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by alamarBlue proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PNPT1 copy numbers decreased more than 10-fold at 9 cm rectal biopsies after 7 days of tenofovir treatment (mean fold change 0.09, 95% CI 0.009–0.172, p < 0.001).
source: PNPT1 copy numbers decreased more than 10-fold at 9 cm (mean fold change 0.09, 95% CI 0.009–0.172, p < 0.001) and by half at 15 cm (0.53, 0.34–0.73, p < 0.001) after 7 days of treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PNPT1 copy numbers decreased by half at 15 cm rectal biopsies after 7 days of tenofovir treatment (0.53, 0.34–0.73, p < 0.001).
source: PNPT1 copy numbers decreased more than 10-fold at 9 cm (mean fold change 0.09, 95% CI 0.009–0.172, p < 0.001) and by half at 15 cm (0.53, 0.34–0.73, p < 0.001) after 7 days of treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ATP6 mRNA copy numbers decreased on average threefold after a single tenofovir application (p = 0.003) and sixfold after 7 days (p < 0.001) in 9 cm rectal biopsies.
source: ATP6 mRNA copy numbers decreased on average threefold (p = 0.003) after a single application and sixfold after 7 days (p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ATP6 copy numbers were stable in all 15 study participants treated with 2% N-9 gel (p = 0.491).
source: In contrast, ATP6 copy numbers were stable in all 15 study participants treated with 2% N-9 gel (p = 0.491) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RT-ddPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The number of mitochondria per µm2 decreased by more than half after 7 days of tenofovir treatment in two study participants (p < 0.001 for both subjects).
source: The number of mitochondria per µm2 decreased by more than half after 7 days of tenofovir treatment (p < 0.001 for both subjects) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy quantification shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In one participant, mitochondria increased in size by 1.4-fold after 7 days of tenofovir treatment (p < 0.001).
source: In the second participant, mitochondria also increased in size by 1.4-fold (p < 0.001) (Figure 5D) and developed dysmorphic cristae during treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mitochondria developed dysmorphic cristae during tenofovir treatment.
source: In the second participant, mitochondria also increased in size by 1.4-fold (p < 0.001) (Figure 5D) and developed dysmorphic cristae during treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Tenofovir caused statistically significant inhibition of PNPT1 and ATP6 mRNA expression in vaginal epithelial cells.
source: In parallel, tenofovir also caused statistically significant inhibition of PNPT1 and ATP6 mRNA expression in vaginal epithelial cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: 483 proteins were detected consistently at baseline and time point VII by mass spectrometry in rectal secretions.
source: However, 483 proteins were detected consistently at baseline and time point VII by mass spectrometry.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 382 proteins increased in the tenofovir arm vs 112 in the no treatment arm in rectal secretions.
source: 382 proteins increased in the tenofovir arm vs 112 in the no treatment arm (five participants/arm).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Significant increases in individual protein expression were only seen in the tenofovir arm.
source: Among these, significant increases in individual protein expression were only seen in the tenofovir arm (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The top 100 proteins in rectal secretions exhibited an average fold increase of 3.8 (median 3.2, range 1.6–128.7) in the tenofovir arm.
source: The top 100 proteins exhibited an average fold increase of 3.8 (median 3.2, range 1.6–128.7) in the tenofovir arm, listed by p value in Figure 6.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Enrichment analysis of rectal secretion proteins primarily indicated enhancement of cell survival and induction of leukocyte migration by tenofovir.
source: Enrichment analysis primarily indicated enhancement of cell survival and induction of leukocyte migration by tenofovir (Figure 6), which is consistent with our other findings.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Tenofovir gel is being evaluated for vaginal and rectal pre-exposure prophylaxis against HIV transmission.
source: Tenofovir gel is being evaluated for vaginal and rectal pre-exposure prophylaxis against HIV transmission.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as background context.

claim: After seven days of administration, tenofovir 1% gel had broad-ranging effects on the rectal mucosa.
source: After seven days of administration, tenofovir 1% gel had broad-ranging effects on the rectal mucosa, which were more pronounced than, but different from, those of the detergent nonoxynol-9.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by multiple data types throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tenofovir's effects on the rectal mucosa were more pronounced than, but different from, those of nonoxynol-9.
source: After seven days of administration, tenofovir 1% gel had broad-ranging effects on the rectal mucosa, which were more pronounced than, but different from, those of the detergent nonoxynol-9.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by comparative gene expression data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed anti-inflammatory mediators.
source: Tenofovir suppressed anti-inflammatory mediators, increased T cell densities, caused mitochondrial dysfunction, altered regulatory pathways of cell differentiation and survival, and stimulated epithelial cell proliferation.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by gene expression and protein data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tenofovir increased T cell densities in the rectal mucosa.
source: Tenofovir suppressed anti-inflammatory mediators, increased T cell densities, caused mitochondrial dysfunction, altered regulatory pathways of cell differentiation and survival, and stimulated epithelial cell proliferation.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Tenofovir caused mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Tenofovir suppressed anti-inflammatory mediators, increased T cell densities, caused mitochondrial dysfunction, altered regulatory pathways of cell differentiation and survival, and stimulated epithelial cell proliferation.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by mitochondrial gene expression and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tenofovir altered regulatory pathways of cell differentiation and survival.
source: Tenofovir suppressed anti-inflammatory mediators, increased T cell densities, caused mitochondrial dysfunction, altered regulatory pathways of cell differentiation and survival, and stimulated epithelial cell proliferation.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by pathway analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Tenofovir stimulated epithelial cell proliferation.
source: Tenofovir suppressed anti-inflammatory mediators, increased T cell densities, caused mitochondrial dysfunction, altered regulatory pathways of cell differentiation and survival, and stimulated epithelial cell proliferation.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In CAPRISA 004, pericoital tenofovir 1% gel was 39% efficacious in preventing vaginal HIV acquisition.
source: In a phase 2B trial, CAPRISA 004, pericoital tenofovir 1% gel was 39% efficacious in preventing vaginal HIV acquisition (Abdool Karim et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from published clinical trial results.

claim: In the VOICE study (MTN-003), the daily vaginal tenofovir 1% gel arm was discontinued for futility.
source: However, in another phase 2B trial, the VOICE study (MTN-003), the daily vaginal tenofovir 1% gel arm was discontinued for futility (Marrazzo et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published clinical trial results.

claim: Adherence to product use was low in VOICE, likely explaining the differences in findings between CAPRISA 004 and VOICE.
source: Adherence to product use was low in VOICE, likely explaining the differences in findings between the two studies.
evidence: Inference based on cited clinical trial results.

claim: The CAPRISA 004 study is being repeated in a phase 3 trial (FACTS 001 study).
source: Currently, the CAPRISA 004 study is being repeated in a phase 3 trial (FACTS 001 study).
evidence: Statement of ongoing clinical trial.

claim: A reduced glycerin formulation of the vaginal tenofovir 1% gel for use as a rectal microbicide appears safe when evaluated by epithelial sloughing, fecal calprotectin, inflammatory cytokine mRNA/protein levels, and cellular immune activation markers.
source: A reduced glycerin formulation of the vaginal tenofovir 1% gel for use as a rectal microbicide appears safe when evaluated by epithelial sloughing, fecal calprotectin, inflammatory cytokine mRNA/protein levels, and cellular immune activation markers (McGowan et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from published clinical trial results.

claim: Tenofovir did not directly cause inflammation.
source: We did not find evidence that tenofovir directly causes inflammation, which is in keeping with our prior report that rectal tenofovir gel did not cause overt histological inflammation or increased mRNA/protein levels of a select panel of pro-inflammatory cytokines (McGowan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by current study findings and cited prior publication.

claim: Tenofovir dampened anti-inflammatory factors.
source: Rather, tenofovir dampened anti-inflammatory factors.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data showing suppression of IL-10, CREB1, CREBBP, and TGF-β pathways.

claim: Tenofovir strongly inhibited IL-10 gene and protein expression, likely via blocking of CREB1 and its coactivator CREBBP.
source: Most prominently, it strongly inhibited IL-10 gene and protein expression, likely via blocking of CREB1 and its coactivator CREBBP (Martin et al., 2005; Woodgett and Ohashi, 2005; Gee et al., 2006; Alvarez et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and protein data with mechanistic inference based on cited literature.

claim: Tenofovir suppressed signaling pathways downstream of TGF-β.
source: In addition, it suppressed signaling pathways downstream of TGF-β, a central anti-inflammatory mediator in the gut (Konkel and Chen, 2011; Surh and Sprent, 2012).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis with cited literature on TGF-β function.

claim: TGF-β is a central anti-inflammatory mediator in the gut.
source: In addition, it suppressed signaling pathways downstream of TGF-β, a central anti-inflammatory mediator in the gut (Konkel and Chen, 2011; Surh and Sprent, 2012).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: CXCL13 is a B lymphocyte chemoattractant.
source: Consequently, a number of chemokines were induced, such as the B lymphocyte chemoattractant CXCL13 (Ansel et al., 2002), and CCL19 and CCL21, both ligands of CCR7 on T lymphocytes and dendritic cells (Forster et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: CCL19 and CCL21 are both ligands of CCR7 on T lymphocytes and dendritic cells.
source: Consequently, a number of chemokines were induced, such as the B lymphocyte chemoattractant CXCL13 (Ansel et al., 2002), and CCL19 and CCL21, both ligands of CCR7 on T lymphocytes and dendritic cells (Forster et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Tenofovir creates a state of potential hyper-responsiveness to external inflammatory stimuli but does not itself cause inflammation.
source: In concert, these changes suggest that tenofovir creates a state of potential hyper-responsiveness to external inflammatory stimuli but does not itself cause inflammation.
evidence: Inference based on multiple gene expression and protein findings.

claim: In populations with high incidence of mucosal infections and associated immune activation, tenofovir could potentially diminish the anti-viral protective effect of topical tenofovir prophylaxis.
source: In populations who, unlike our MTN-007 study cohort, have a high incidence of mucosal infections and associated immune activation, this could potentially diminish the anti-viral protective effect of topical tenofovir prophylaxis (Naranbhai et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative inference based on study findings and cited literature.

claim: Mitochondrial toxicity of nucleotide/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as tenofovir is well described but the mechanism remains unclear.
source: Mitochondrial toxicity of nucleotide/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as tenofovir is well described but the mechanism remains unclear (Lewis et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: PNPASE regulates nucleus-encoded RNA import into mitochondria.
source: PNPASE regulates nucleus-encoded RNA import into mitochondria (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: In PNPT1 knock-out mice, mitochondrial morphology and respiratory capacity are disrupted in a manner similar to the disruption in renal proximal tubular cells in patients with tenofovir-induced nephrotoxicity.
source: In PNPT1 knock-out mice, mitochondrial morphology and respiratory capacity are disrupted in a manner quite similar to the disruption in renal proximal tubular cells in patients with tenofovir-induced nephrotoxicity (Perazella, 2010; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Tenofovir's suppression of PNPT1 expression may underlie its reported mitochondrial toxicity.
source: These findings suggest that tenofovir's suppression of PNPT1 expression may underlie its reported, but heretofore unexplained, mitochondrial toxicity.
evidence: Inference based on study findings and cited literature on PNPT1 function.

claim: Tenofovir's negative effect on mitochondrial function could lead to impairment of tumor progenitor cell apoptosis.
source: Furthermore, tenofovir's negative effect on mitochondrial function could lead to impairment of tumor progenitor cell apoptosis (Modica-Napolitano et al., 2007; Ni Chonghaile et al., 2011), as has been specifically reported for loss-of-function mutations of mtATP6, a mitochondrial gene strongly suppressed by tenofovir in our study (Shidara et al., 2005).
evidence: Speculative inference based on study findings and cited literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of mtATP6 lead to impairment of tumor progenitor cell apoptosis.
source: Furthermore, tenofovir's negative effect on mitochondrial function could lead to impairment of tumor progenitor cell apoptosis (Modica-Napolitano et al., 2007; Ni Chonghaile et al., 2011), as has been specifically reported for loss-of-function mutations of mtATP6, a mitochondrial gene strongly suppressed by tenofovir in our study (Shidara et al., 2005).
